prompt: Design a lifecycle-safe migration for a Unity 6 co-op game that creates Addressables-backed projectile prefabs with InstantiateAsync and destroys them after impact. A Development Player capture shows recurring managed allocation during bursts. The proposed solution is an ObjectPool of projectile components plus a reused Physics.OverlapSphereNonAlloc array for damage. Peak concurrent projectiles are believed to be 128 but only 64 were observed; the damage buffer holds 32 colliders and sometimes returns a full buffer. Each projectile owns event subscriptions, a PrimeTween trail fade, and a UniTask homing loop bound to scene lifetime. Additive combat scenes unload while Addressables operations may still be completing, and Domain Reload is disabled in the Editor. Provide a test-first migration and ownership protocol covering pool warm-up/capacity/exhaustion, dirty reset, cancellation and late callbacks, Addressables reference counts, full buffer truncation/order/fallback, scene/domain teardown, retained/native memory, rollback, and representative target-player verification.
assertions: The response defines one owner for the pool, Addressables load handle, active/inactive projectiles, damage buffer, and teardown, with acquisition and release paired exactly once.

Capacity distinguishes observed 64, believed peak 128, warm-up, max size, retained-memory cap, empty-pool exhaustion, overflow behavior, growth telemetry, and remeasurement rather than treating 128 as proven.

Get/release/reset/destroy behavior covers transforms, physics, visual/material state, subscriptions, PrimeTween cancellation/reset, UniTask cancellation, retained references, and a fresh lease generation or equivalent late-callback safeguard.
Addressables instance/load APIs and reference counts are paired according to the installed package, and pooled instances cannot outlive the asset or bundle handle they depend on.
Additive scene unload stops new leases, handles in-flight completion/cancellation races, settles active/inactive objects, rejects late returns deterministically, and releases handles in a safe order.
A full buffer is detected and receives an explicit tested truncation, ordering, telemetry, and fallback policy; the response does not assume the 32 results are nearest or complete.

Tests begin with meaningful functional red cases and cover dirty reuse, exhaustion, overflow, double return, use after return, scene unload, Domain Reload configuration, cancellation, and Addressables late completion.
Allocation red and green use the same representative burst workload after warm-up in a target player across all relevant threads, without placing test assertion overhead inside the measured window.

Managed allocation, pool-retained memory, Addressables residency, native physics memory, and CPU are measured separately, with rollback triggers if correctness, saturation, memory, or frame-time budgets fail.
